title: First fault-tolerant quantum memory demonstration for a generalized superfast encoding
abstract: The Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) is a fermion-to-qubit mapping that has error-correcting/detecting properties. To this point, all demonstrations have been relegated to error-detection only, as no fault-tolerance under circuit-level noise has been observed. Here, we introduce an even-distance $d$ constant stabilizer-weight GSE where each of $N$ modes is assigned a $d$-qubit block arranged on a ring. The resulting stabilizer generators have constant weight 4 or 6 for any even distance $d$. Furthermore, the full stabilizer set of this construction can always be partitioned into four qubit-wise commuting groups, which enables compact syndrome-extraction scheduling. We simulate quantum memory experiments under circuit-level depolarizing noise for two instances of this code, $[[48,8,6]]$ and $[[64,8,8]]$ and the threshold is observed to be $\approx 4\times10^{-3}$. This is, to our knowledge, the first fault-tolerant quantum-memory characterization of a fermion-mapping with threshold-like scaling.
summary: This work introduces a novel, constant-weight Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) designed for fault-tolerant quantum memory of fermionic systems. By simulating performance under circuit noise, the authors report the first observation of threshold-like scaling for such a fermion-mapping, achieving a threshold around $4 	imes 10^{-3}$. This advances the practical feasibility of using quantum error correction for simulating fermionic quantum matter.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of demonstrating fault-tolerant quantum memory specifically for a fermion-to-qubit mapping.
main_result: They achieved a simulation showing a threshold-like scaling for fault tolerance at a physical error rate of approximately $4 	imes 10^{-3}$ for two specific code instances.
method: The authors constructed an even-distance, constant stabilizer-weight Generalized Superfast Encoding (GSE) and simulated quantum memory operations under circuit-level depolarizing noise.
model_or_system: The system involves encoding fermionic modes into qubits using the GSE, which utilizes stabilizer generators with weights of 4 or 6. The simulation tests two specific stabilizer codes: $[[48, 8, 6]]$ and $[[64, 8, 8]]$.
key_observables: Logical error rate ($ ar{\epsilon}_L(p)$) as a function of the physical depolarizing error rate ($p$).
important_parameters: The observed threshold is $\approx 4 	imes 10^{-3}$. The tested codes have distances $d=6$ and $d=8$, and logical qubits $k=8$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on simulating circuit-level depolarizing noise and assumes the applicability of the developed GSE structure for fault tolerance.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the logical error rate ($ ar{\epsilon}_L(p)$) for both tested codes versus $p$, illustrating the approach to a pseudo-threshold near $p \approx 4 	imes 10^{-3}$.
paper_structure: The paper details the construction of the constant-weight GSE stabilizers, analyzes the operator weights using 'a' and 'b' families of local Majorana operators, and simulates the memory performance using AlphaSyndrome extraction and Relay-BP decoding.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, simulated demonstration of fault tolerance for a fermion-mapping, which is crucial for quantum simulation efforts involving fermionic Hamiltonians.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Logical error rate per round per logical qubit versus physical depolarizing error rate p, for the [[48, 8, 6]] and [[64, 8, 8]] even-weight GSE codes, decoded with Relay-BP using AlphaSyndrome- scheduled syndrome extraction. Solid curves are log-log power-law fits to each code’s data. The dashed line is the unencoded (physical) error rate for reference. The higher-distance code suppresses logical error more strongly at low p with the two curves approaching each other near p ≈4 × 10−3.
